d.title: One path object, nine answers, and no string slicing
d.caption: **Treat a path as a string and you take responsibility for its structure — separators, duplicates, trailing slashes, platform differences — and the wrongness usually only appears on the other operating system.** `Path` models the structure instead: **`/` joins with the correct separator, and the parts you would otherwise parse out are attributes.** The two rows worth noticing are `suffix` and `suffixes`: **`.gz` alone, or `['.tar', '.gz']` for the pair** — which is the distinction a `rsplit(".")` gets wrong on `orders.tar.gz`.

d.title: The same code reads the same file differently on two machines
d.caption: **Until Python 3.15, `open()` without `encoding` uses whatever the operating system says the local default is — UTF-8 on modern Linux and macOS, cp1252 on a Western Windows install, cp932 on a Japanese one.** Which is the mechanism behind **the single most common cross-platform Python bug**, and the traceback shows its shape: `'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x9d`. The three arguments to know: **`utf-8-sig` for anything out of Excel, or your first column name becomes `\ufeffid`; `surrogateescape` to round-trip undecodable filenames; and `newline=""`, which the `csv` module requires.**

d.title: Two rows that split into five, three and two fields, none of them right
d.caption: **CSV looks like a format you can parse in one line and it is not: a field may be quoted, a quoted field may contain a comma, a newline, or a quote escaped by doubling it.** The naive split produces `['1001', '"Acme', ' Inc."', '', '49.99']` — **one record become five fields with stray quotes** — and the second record splits across two lines because a quoted field contained a newline. `DictReader` gets all four cases right: **`'Acme, Inc.'`, `'O"Brien Ltd'`, and a notes field containing an actual newline.**

d.title: A JSON array is only valid once its closing bracket has been read
d.caption: **`json.load(f)` builds the entire document before returning — there is no partial parse and no streaming mode, because a JSON array is only valid once its closing bracket arrives.** So a 4 GB array costs 4 GB of file **plus the considerably larger in-memory object graph.** **JSON Lines removes the problem without a new library: one complete JSON object per line, no enclosing array, no commas between records** — so every line is independently parseable and the file streams in constant memory, **and a truncated file loses one record rather than all of them.**

d.title: A documented part of the object model, and nothing checks what it returns
d.caption: **`__reduce__` is a supported hook that tells `pickle` how to rebuild an object — any class can define it, and nothing validates the callable it names.** So a class whose `__reduce__` returns `(os.system, ("...",))` produces a 60-byte pickle that **runs arbitrary code as you, during `load()`, before you have looked at a single value.** The bytes are readable in the output: **`posix` and `system` appear as plain strings in the stream** — which is also what makes §03's `find_class` override possible.

d.title: Seven formats, and only one of them executes on load
d.caption: **The MAC does not make pickle safe — it makes the pickle unloadable unless someone with your key produced it**, which is a different and sufficient claim. And overriding `find_class` works because **every `GLOBAL` opcode routes through it**, giving `_pickle.UnpicklingError: blocked global: posix.system`. The table's real content is the first column: **pickle is the only row that executes on load, and the bottom four have a schema** — with `safetensors` built specifically to replace pickled checkpoints.

state: compact binary on a hot path

d.title: A pickle does not contain your class — it contains the import path of your class
d.caption: **Rebuilding the object requires that path to still resolve to a compatible definition**, which is why `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'myapp.model'` is the normal end state of an archived pickle. Four things break it, and the second is the quiet one: **an added attribute is simply missing rather than defaulted, because `__setstate__` only restores the keys present in the stream** — so the failure surfaces later, somewhere else. And the fourth fails at **load, not at build**: a protocol-5 pickle is unreadable by 3.7.

d.title: An absolute import says where something comes from without counting dots
d.caption: **Absolute imports say where something comes from without the reader counting dots, and they survive a file being moved** — which is why PEP 8 recommends them. Explicit relative imports earn their place in one case: **inside a package that may be vendored or renamed, where `from .models import Order` keeps working after the package is re-rooted.** The form to avoid entirely is the implicit relative import, **which Python 3 removed** — and the reason it was removed is that `import models` inside a package was ambiguous with a top-level `models`.

nodes.label: And survives the file being moved

d.title: Every `__init__.py` on the path runs first
d.caption: **Three levels of package means three files execute before the one you asked for** — which is why a heavy import at the top of a package's `__init__.py` is paid by anyone importing anything beneath it, including a test that wanted one helper. The practical rule follows: **keep `__init__.py` to re-exports and `__all__`, and put the work in the modules.** And the modern detail: **a directory without `__init__.py` is still importable as a namespace package**, which is useful for plugins and a trap when it silences a typo'd directory name.

d.title: Four levels of visibility, and one of them means nothing at module level
d.caption: **A single underscore is a convention, not a mechanism — `_name` is importable and you may change it without notice, which is exactly why you should use it liberally: an internal helper marked `_` is one you can refactor freely.** The row to avoid is the third: **double underscores are name-mangled inside a class only, so `__helper` at module level is just a confusing name** with no privacy. And the fourth is the one people miss: **a name absent from `__all__` is outside the documented API even without an underscore.**

d.title: Activation only edits PATH, so you never actually need to activate
d.caption: **The interpreter finds its environment by reading `pyvenv.cfg` next to the executable — which is why `.venv/bin/python script.py` works with no activation at all.** Activation is a convenience for an interactive shell, and **the explicit path is safer in scripts and CI**, where an unactivated or wrongly activated shell is a class of failure that simply cannot happen if you name the interpreter. Which also explains 1.2's diagnostic: **`sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix` reads that same config file.**

d.title: Seven specifiers, and the bare lower bound is the one to stop writing
d.caption: **`>=2.31` allows anything newer *including 3.0*, so it is rarely correct on its own — the next major release will break you and the install will succeed.** The right default for a direct dependency is **`>=2.31,<3`**, or `~=2.31` which means the same thing more compactly. And the first row is a rule rather than a preference: **`==` belongs in a lockfile and never in a library's dependencies**, because an exact pin in a library makes it uninstallable alongside anything else that pinned differently.

d.title: Five fields, and two of them are where projects go wrong
d.caption: **Bound `requires-python` on both sides — without an upper bound, `pip` will happily install into a Python released after your code was written and fail at runtime instead of at install time.** And **`dynamic = ["version"]` says the backend computes it; the alternative is a version written twice, here and in `__init__.py`, which drifts apart the first time someone is in a hurry.** The naming row is worth getting right once: **`acme-billing` on the index and `acme_billing` in code — the index normalises hyphens, underscores and case, and the import name is whatever directory you ship.**

d.title: Three tables, and only one of them is not shipped to your users
d.caption: **The third column is the distinction that matters: `dependencies` and extras travel in the published metadata, and `[dependency-groups]` does not.** Which makes the choice mechanical rather than stylistic: **anything a user might need is a dependency or an extra; anything only a developer needs is a group.** Putting pytest in `optional-dependencies` is the common mistake — **it then appears on the index as a feature your users can install**, and it is why `[dependency-groups]` was added.

state: what the code needs to run

d.title: Six backends, and the choice is made by what you are building
d.caption: **hatchling is the default for a new pure-Python project — fast, sensible defaults, good version handling, no legacy surface.** The row that overrides it is the second: **setuptools is the only one with deep extension-building support**, so a C extension decides the question for you and you pay in configuration. The last three are decided by the language you are extending: **maturin for Rust and PyO3, scikit-build-core for a CMake-based C++ extension** — which replaces the setuptools-plus-CMake dance. And for pdm or poetry: **fine, just do not mix them.**

state: a single module, no build steps

d.title: Two modules, and choosing the wrong one is a security bug rather than a style one
d.caption: **`uuid4` is random and `uuid5` is a deterministic hash of a namespace and a name — so the same inputs always give the same id, which is what you want for an idempotency key derived from a request.** The `secrets` rows are the ones to get right: **`token_urlsafe` and `token_hex` are cryptographically secure, and `random` is not** — `random.choice` for a password reset token is a real vulnerability, because Mersenne Twister's state is recoverable from its output. **And `compare_digest` is constant-time, which `==` on a token is not.**

d.title: A complete SQL database in the standard library, and two defaults to change
d.caption: **`sqlite3` stores everything in one file — no server, no configuration, no dependency — and it is the right answer far more often than people expect: a local cache, a desktop application's storage, a scratch database in a script, and above all tests, where `:memory:` gives you a real database per test.** Two defaults to change immediately: **`row_factory = sqlite3.Row`, without which every result is positional**, and the transaction behaviour — **it does not autocommit the way you expect**, so a script that forgets to commit writes nothing and reports nothing.

d.title: Eight dependencies the standard library has replaced, and two it has not
d.caption: **`zoneinfo` replaced `pytz` outright in 3.9 and with a saner API; `tomllib` replaced TOML readers in 3.11, read-only; and `six` and `future` replaced nothing, because Python 2 compatibility ended in 2020.** The two rows where the package still wins are worth being honest about: **`urllib.request` is grudging for a single GET and `httpx` is worth it for anything real**, and **`orjson` earns its place only when profiling says serialisation is the bottleneck** — which is rarer than the benchmark posts suggest.
